description_full: GO Residential Real Estate Investment Trust is an internally managed, open ended real estate investment trust established under, and governed by, the laws of the Province of Ontario. The REIT has been formed to provide investors with an opportunity to invest in luxury high-rise multifamily properties (LHRs) located in the New York metropolitan area and other major metropolitan cities in the United States. The REIT owns and operates a portfolio of eight LHRs consisting of 2,731 luxury suites located in New York City, New York. GO Residential Real Estate Investment Trust was established on June 13, 2025 and incorporated in Ontario, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. Joshua  Gotlib | CEO, Chief Investment Officer & Trustee | Age 40 | Compensation: $8.3M (FY2025)
financial_summary: Go Residential Real Estate Inve is a small-cap real estate business with a $311M market cap on $153M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +2.5pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 65% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $100M in free cash flow — roughly 65 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.17×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +18.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 15.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.9× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 58% operating margin runs 35pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.89x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
val: The stock trades 85% below its DCF fair value of $49.15, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 79%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $30.25 to $77.28 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on P/FCF 3.1 vs 17.8, richer on EV/EBITDA 31.7 vs 16.3 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 32.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 7.2% annual cash-flow growth, 13pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.21).
It runs a 65% gross margin and converts 65% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9, but cash conversion of only 0.17x and high accruals (+18.8% of assets).
ROE of 57% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 68% last year, worth watching.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 15.2x net debt to EBITDA ($6.5M of cash against $1.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.9x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.60 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.54 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
The Beneish M-score (-1.99) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.3% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 4.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 18.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 14%.
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (8.8% in dividends, less 7.0% of net share issuance).
